**2.6 Data Gathering Procedures**

The data-gathering procedures of the study were conducted in two phases: preliminary requirements gathering and final system evaluation. During the preliminary requirements-gathering phase, household decision-makers participated in an online needs-analysis survey distributed through social media platforms using Google Forms. One-on-one synchronous interviews were conducted with barangay officials, while field experts participated through synchronous or asynchronous interviews depending on their professional availability. The data obtained from these participants were used to identify user needs, local contextual factors, technical requirements, and system design considerations prior to and during the development of LUMI.  
The final system-evaluation phase was conducted after the development and deployment of the working LUMI prototype. This phase involved 100 household end users from Region IV-A, 10 IT experts, and five engineering experts. The specific procedures used for these groups are discussed under Section 2.8, Testing and Evaluation.

**2.6.1 Preliminary Needs Analysis Survey**

During the preliminary requirements-gathering phase, the study utilized an online needs-analysis survey to gather information from household decision-makers. The instrument was administered online through Google Forms and distributed via social media platforms to reach respondents who met the study's eligibility criteria. The questionnaire contains structured, close-ended questions that are quantifiable, using checkboxes for multiple-response items, yes-or-no questions, and a five-point Likert scale ranging from Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree, allowing responses to be aggregated and analyzed statistically. For the online needs analysis survey, a total of 196 respondents participated.

The survey is organized into five parts, each addressed in the corresponding subsections below: 

* 2.6.1.1 Respondent Profile  
* 2.6.1.2 Problem Identification  
* 2.6.1.3 User Requirements   
* 2.6.1.4 System Requirements   
* 2.6.1.5 User Needs and Preferences

**2.6.1.2 Problem Identification** 

This section identifies the problems and concerns related to the respondents' current electricity source, costs, and supply issues.

![][image7]  
*Figure 2.9: Experience with Electricity Problems (Pie Chart)*

Out of the 196 people who took part in the survey, 174, about 88.8% shared that they were facing issues with their current electricity source. On the flip side, 22 respondents, making up 11.2%, said they didn’t have any problems. This data highlights that electricity-related issues are quite prevalent among the household decision-makers surveyed, which sets the stage for exploring their interest in renewable energy options.

![][image8]  
*Figure 2.10: Current Concerns with Electricity Source (Horizontal Bar Chart)*

Among the concerns respondents raised regarding their existing electricity source, price or cost was the most frequently cited, selected by 179 respondents (91.3%), followed by unreliability at 106 respondents (54.1%). Lack of alternatives to sources was selected by 50 respondents (25.5%), while lack of control was the least cited concern at 17 respondents (8.7%). As respondents were allowed to select multiple concerns, these results indicate that cost is the predominant driver of dissatisfaction, considerably ahead of supply reliability and other factors.

Nearly all respondents, 195 out of 196 (99.5%), reported that electricity price increases have affected their household expenses, with only a single respondent (0.5%) indicating otherwise. This near-unanimous result underscores the financial burden of rising electricity costs on CALABARZON households and reinforces cost reduction as a central motivation for considering renewable energy alternatives.

![][image10]

An overwhelming majority of the respondents 192 out of 196, or 98.0% shared that they were looking into alternative or renewable energy sources. On the flip side, just four respondents, making up 2.0%, said they weren't considering these options. This clearly shows a strong interest in renewable energy among those surveyed. However, it's important to note that just because people are interested doesn't mean they're actually making the switch to renewable energy.

**2.6.1.3 User Requirements** 

This section determines the respondents' interest in renewable energy solutions and the underlying reasons motivating that interest.

| Weighted Mean Range  | Verbal Interpretation |
| :---: | :---: |
| 4.20 \- 5.00  | Strongly Agree/Very Likely  |
| 3.40 \- 4.19  | Agree/Likely  |
| 2.60 \- 3.39  | Neutral |
| 1.80 \- 2.59  | Disagree/Unlikely   |
| 1.00 \- 1.79  | Strongly Disagree/Very Unlikely  |

*Table 2.8. Weighted Mean Interpretation Scale*

The weighted mean results for the Likert-scale and ordinal items were interpreted using the five-level scale shown above. The interval width of 0.80 was derived by dividing the range between the highest and lowest scale values by the number of response categories, that is, (5 − 1\) ÷ 5 \= 0.80. This scale was applied to interpret both agreement-based items (Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree) and likelihood-based items (Very Unlikely to Very Likely), as both used the same five-point structure.

| Section  | Statement  | Weighted Mean  | Verbal Interpretation  |

*Table 2.9: Weighted Mean \- Selected Likert and Ordinal Items* 

The respondents generally agreed or strongly agreed across all measured statements, with weighted means ranging from 3.80 to 4.69. The statement "The system should be easy to use and understand" received the highest weighted mean at 4.69 (Strongly Agree), indicating that usability is a near-universal expectation among respondents. This was followed by the 5-year renewable energy adoption likelihood at 4.49 (Very Likely) and trust in system-generated recommendations at 4.47 (Very Likely), both reflecting strong respondent confidence in adopting renewable energy and in relying on an automated recommendation system. The statement "The initial cost of renewable energy affects my decision to adopt it"   
recorded a weighted mean of 4.31 (Strongly Agree), reinforcing cost as a decisive factor in adoption behavior. The lowest weighted mean in this group, 3.80 (Agree), corresponded to the statement "The electricity supply in my area is unreliable," suggesting that while reliability concerns are present, they are perceived as less urgent than cost and usability considerations among respondents.

![][image11]  
*Figure 2.13: Reasons for Considering Renewable Energy (Horizontal Bar Chart)*

Among the reasons respondents cited for considering renewable energy, reducing electricity bills was the most common, selected by 191 respondents (97.4%), followed by avoiding power interruptions at 149 respondents (76.0%). Helping the environment was selected by 89 respondents (45.4%), while achieving energy independence was the least cited reason at 65 respondents (33.2%). As respondents could select multiple reasons, these results indicate that financial motivation, rather than environmental concern, is the primary driver behind respondents' interest in renewable energy.

**2.6.1.4 System Requirements** 

This section identifies the features, tasks, and outputs expected of a system that recommends renewable energy sources. 

*![][image12]*  
*Figure 2.14: Desired Features of the System (Horizontal Bar Chart)*

Renewable energy source recommendations emerged as the most desired feature, selected by 180 respondents (91.8%), followed by estimated installation and maintenance costs at 149 respondents (76.0%). Monthly energy savings estimation was selected by 128 respondents (65.3%), and energy consumption monitoring and analysis by 110 respondents (56.1%). Power interruption or backup power recommendations and environmental impact and benefit analysis were selected by 78 (39.8%) and 77 (39.3%) respondents respectively, while what-if simulation and comparison of energy options was the least selected feature at 58 respondents (29.6%). These results suggest that respondents prioritize direct, actionable recommendations and cost-related information over more exploratory or simulation-based features.

![][image13]  
*Figure 2.15: Desired System Tasks (Horizontal Bar Chart)*

Respondents most frequently desired that the system analyze household energy consumption, selected by 159 respondents (81.1%), followed by recommending suitable renewable energy sources at 151 respondents (77.0%). Estimating installation and operating costs was selected by 127 respondents (64.8%), while comparing current electricity usage with renewable energy options was selected by 110 respondents (56.1%). Forecasting future energy demand and expenses and providing backup power recommendations during outages were selected by 87 (44.4%) and 88 (44.9%) respondents respectively, while simulating and comparing different renewable energy scenarios was the least selected task at 70 respondents (35.7%). This pattern mirrors the desired features results, reinforcing that respondents place greater value on consumption-based analysis and direct recommendations than on simulation-based functionality.

![][image14]  
*Figure 2.16: Willingness to use the System (Pie Chart)*

Out of the 196 people surveyed, a whopping 179 (91.3%) said they would definitely consider using a system that suggests the best renewable energy sources for their homes. Meanwhile, 17 respondents (8.7%) mentioned they might give it a try. Interestingly, no one said they wouldn’t use it at all. These results point to a positive initial interest among those surveyed in a renewable energy recommendation system. However, it’s important to note that these findings don’t assess how user-friendly or widely accepted the finished LUMI system actually is.

![][image15]  
*Figure 2.17: Desired System Outputs (Horizontal Bar Chart)* 

Estimated installation cost was the most desired system output, selected by 174 respondents (88.8%), followed by recommended renewable energy type at 155 respondents (79.1%). Estimated monthly savings was selected by 132 respondents (67.3%), and power generation estimates by 118 respondents (60.2%). Environmental benefits, return on investment analysis, and maintenance requirements were selected by 90 (45.9%), 81 (41.3%), and 79 (40.3%) respondents respectively. These results show that respondents are most interested in outputs with direct cost implications, consistent with the cost-driven motivations identified throughout the survey.

**2.6.1.5 User Needs and Preferences** 

This section determines the respondents’ existing knowledge of renewable energy, the factors influencing their adoption decisions, and their likelihood of adopting renewable energy and trusting a system-generated recommendation.   
![][image16]  
*Figure 2.18: Factors Considered in Choosing a Renewable Energy Source (Horizontal Bar Chart)* 

Initial installation cost was the most frequently considered factor when choosing a renewable energy source, selected by 170 respondents (86.7%), followed closely by monthly electricity savings at 167 respondents (85.2%). Reliability and consistency of energy supply was selected by 140 respondents (71.4%), while environmental impact and sustainability was selected by 100 respondents (51.0%). Maintenance requirements and availability of space for installation were selected by 92 (46.9%) and 75 (38.3%) respondents respectively. These results further confirm that cost-related factors, both upfront and ongoing, weigh most heavily in respondents' renewable energy decision-making.

*Table 2.10: Weighted Mean Interpretation Scale (6-point)* 

We looked at the weighted mean for the renewable-energy knowledge item using a six-point scale. To figure out the interval width, we took the difference between the highest and lowest values on the scale and divided it by the number of response categories. This gave us (6 − 1\) ÷ 6 ≈ 0.83. We then used these interpretation intervals to categorize how respondents rated their own knowledge of renewable-energy sources.

*Table 2.11: Weighted Mean \- Current Knowledge on Renewable Energy Sources* 

Respondents reported a weighted mean of 2.92 for their current knowledge of renewable energy sources, which falls within the Basic Understanding range (2.67–3.49). This result indicates that, on average, respondents possess only a foundational awareness of renewable energy concepts, despite the strong interest in adoption and high trust in system-generated recommendations observed elsewhere in the survey. This gap between limited technical knowledge and strong adoption interest reinforces the relevance of a guided recommendation system such as LUMI, which can support users in making informed renewable energy decisions without requiring them to possess advanced prior knowledge.

![][image17]  
*Figure 2.19: Renewable Energy Sources of Interest (Horizontal Bar Chart)* 

Solar energy was overwhelmingly the most preferred renewable energy source, selected by 194 respondents (99.0%), followed by wind energy at 99 respondents (50.5%) and hydropower at 54 respondents (27.6%). Geothermal energy and biomass energy were selected by 20 (10.2%) and 15 (7.7%) respondents respectively, while only 1 respondent (0.5%) indicated unfamiliarity with renewable energy sources. The near-universal preference for solar suggests respondents' interest in renewable energy is heavily solar-centric, which may have implications for how LUMI presents and balances recommendations across the full range of renewable energy types it supports.

*Table 2.12 Summary of Recurring Themes Across Barangay Official Interviews*

This table presents a cross-respondent thematic synthesis of interviews conducted with four barangay officials representing each of the study's selected reference locations: Bulacan (Sta. Ines), Camarines Sur (Sabang), Leyte (Matin-ao), and Eastern Samar (Barbo). Solar consistently emerged as the most preferred renewable energy source across all four sites, with each respondent grounding this preference in direct, lived exposure. Disaster resilience and cost savings were likewise cited as motivating factors across all sites, though emphasis varied, with more concrete disaster-response use cases in typhoon-prone Eastern Samar and Leyte, and a more cost-centered framing in Bulacan and Camarines Sur.

Community openness was rated high overall, though not uniformly maximal: Bulacan and Camarines Sur officials reported full confidence (5/5), while Leyte and Eastern Samar withheld a perfect score due to unresolved process clarity rather than resistance. All four respondents indicated that consultation and transparency were necessary preconditions for endorsement, though specific requirements varied by site.

The table also surfaces meaningful divergence, particularly in environmental protection status, ranging from total river protection in Bulacan, to informal sensitivity in Camarines Sur, to partial protection plus fault-line risk in Leyte, to unconfirmed status in Eastern Samar, reflecting the study's deliberate selection of sites with distinct constraint profiles. Three respondents, from Leyte, Camarines Sur, and Eastern Samar, also proposed criteria beyond LUMI's four core dimensions, both centered on typhoon resilience. Together, these findings suggest that while household-level motivations for adoption are broadly consistent across sites, the physical, environmental, and governance conditions determining site suitability vary substantially, reinforcing the need for LUMI's site-specific, data-driven assessment approach.

*Table 2.13 Summary of Recurring Themes Across Field Experts*

The table 2.13 highlighted the key themes identified in the interviews conducted with field experts. Two of the four respondents indicated a strong preference to solar energy sources and have provided responses focused on solar energy. The reliability of the source can affect the trust of the users, with respondents pivoting towards credible government-vetted, or internationally-recognized organizations. The recency of the data itself is also key in adopting towards handling changing climate.  The respondents also preferred a dual-interface design meant to cater towards novice and expert users. The accuracy threshold must also be at least 80% according to respondents depending on the usage of the system, with higher stake decision making requiring 90-95% accuracy. The Fuzzy AHP and TOPSIS are seen as the strongest recommendation for MCDM, particularly a hybrid of the two methods. Audit trails and decision history are also seen by half of the respondents as necessary.

**2.6.3 Document Reviews** 

To support the development and contextual relevance of the platform, the researchers conducted a review of academic literature, institutional materials and government reports related to renewable energy, environmental intelligence, energy forecasting and machine learning applications in the domain of energy. This included research papers, energy forecasting studies, government energy reports, machine learning methodology references and environmental datasets documentation published between 2021 and 2025\. The reviewed documents provided theoretical grounding for algorithm selection, renewable energy formulas and system architecture. 

**2.6.4 Observation**

Alongside surveys and interviews, the researchers took a more hands-on approach by informally observing renewable-energy installations in their local areas. They checked out solar panels on everything from residential rooftops to commercial buildings and shopping malls. These observations helped paint a clearer picture of how solar-energy technologies are visibly integrated into the community. However, it’s important to note that these observations weren’t part of a formal procedure and weren’t intended to measure renewable-energy adoption rates or confirm the survey results.

**2.6.5 Testing Scripts / Code**

To ensure system reliability, accuracy and functionality, the researchers conducted a series of internal tests using pre-written scripts and manual walkthroughs. The testing process included debugging, validating logic flows and checking system components such as machine learning model functionalities, API responses and the interactivity of the modules. Functional testing and basic unit testing were applied to identify errors and verify expected outputs. The test results guided refinements and adjustments to the platform’s backend and user interface before deployment. All code-related changes were version-controlled for traceability.   
**2.7 System Development Procedures**

**2.7.1 Planning**  
**2.7.1.1 Project Schedule : Gantt Chart**   
**![][image18]**  
*Figure 2.20: Gantt Chart*  
**2.7.1.2 Feasibility Study**  
**2.7.1.2.1 Development and Operational Cost:**

The system has been developed with minimal financial cost due to its reliance on free-tier services for hosting and frameworks. But, the system needed cloud hosting to be deployed. The free tier for the infrastructure provided by Supabase for online database services, Render for the backend deployment and Vercel for frontend deployment was sufficient for development and testing. However, during deployment, operations and a possibility of scaling or exceeding usage limits, a Pro tier was necessary to ensure uptime and functionality across multiple users.

**2.7.1.2.2 Benefits and Return of Investment**

LUMI provides potential benefits for households by providing tailored, location-specific assessments of renewable energy options. This includes a look at solar, wind, and hydropower alternatives, along with estimates of energy generation and insights into potential financial and environmental benefits. While the system is built for use across the country at both provincial and municipal levels, its formal evaluation for households took place in Region IV-A (CALABARZON). For its initial commercialization efforts, Metro Manila has been pinpointed as a key target market, especially for homeowners and those making household decisions. Additionally, micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) could be a promising customer segment down the line. However, it’s worth noting that the study didn’t delve into commercial applications or provide verified estimates for revenue and return on investment. So, further market validation and financial assessments will be essential to gauge the commercial viability of this initiative.

**2.7.1.2.3 Commercialization and Monetization Plan**

LUMI's proposed strategy for commercialization includes providing basic renewable-energy assessments for free, with Google AdSense as a potential avenue for generating advertising revenue. Looking ahead, there could be opportunities to monetize through subscription services and one-time payments for extra system features, aligning with the project's implementation plan. As the project evolves, we might also consider expanding into commercial applications and forming partnerships with renewable-energy service providers. However, these strategies are still in the proposal stage, and their success will hinge on actual user demand, people's willingness to pay, operational costs, and ongoing system development and validation.

**2.7.2 Software Design**  
**2.7.2.1 Conceptual Design**  
**![][image19]**  
*Figure 2.21: Conceptual Design*

Figure 2.21 showcases the conceptual design of LUMI, highlighting how its key components interact with one another. Users can navigate the system via a web interface that features sections like Home, About, EnergyHub, and EcoSim. The Home and About pages offer a general overview of the system, while EnergyHub dives into environmental and energy-related data, showcasing renewable energy potential and national energy demand forecasts through engaging visualizations. On the other hand, EcoSim lets users pick a municipality and input relevant household details to create initial renewable energy assessments and comparisons. Both modules tap into the system's environmental intelligence processes and utilize stored datasets to deliver insights that aid households in making informed decisions.

**2.7.2.2 Technical Design:**  
**2.7.2.2.1 Context Data Flow Diagram:**  
**![][image20]**  
*Figure 2.22: Context Data Flow Diagram \- User*

Figure 2.22 presents the Context Data Flow Diagram (Level 0 DFD) for the LUMI system. This diagram represents LUMI as a single process and shows the data flows exchanged between the system and its external entity, the User, without detailing the system's internal processes. The User initiates four types of requests: a Home page request and About page request to retrieve general system information, and an Energy Hub location selection or Ecosim location selection to submit a location for analysis. In response, LUMI returns a system introduction for general navigation requests, regional climate, energy intelligence, and forecast data for Energy Hub queries, and a current and recommended energy comparison for Ecosim queries.

![][image21]  
*Figure 2.23: Context Data Flow Diagram \- Admin*

Figure 2.23 presents the Context Data Flow Diagram (Level 0 DFD) for the Admin actor's interaction with the LUMI system, showing the data flows exchanged between the Admin and the system as a single process, without detailing internal operations. The Admin initiates five types of requests: login credentials to authenticate, user management commands to manage user accounts, an analytics request to view system usage, a configuration update to modify system settings, and a moderation request to review flagged content. In response, LUMI returns an authenticated session or access denial based on the login attempt and role verification, a user list and confirmation following user management actions, usage metrics for the analytics request, an updated system configuration after changes are applied, and a flagged session list for moderation review.

**2.7.2.2.2 Top-Down Data Flow Diagram**  
**![][image22]**  
*Figure 2.24: Top-Down Data Flow Diagram*

Figure 2.24 presents the Top-Down Data Flow Diagram (Level 1 DFD) for the LUMI system, showing how a user's request branches into two independent pipelines after accessing the navigation menu (1.0). In the first pipeline, the user selects Energy Hub (2.0) and specifies a geographic level, municipality or province (3.0), which Process 4.0 uses to query the database and return a choropleth map of renewable energy suitability scores. In the second pipeline, the user selects Ecosim (5.0) and inputs a specific municipality (6.0), which Process 7.0 uses to query the database and return a comparison between current and recommended renewable energy options. Both pipelines operate independently but draw from the same shared renewable\_site\_DB, which centralizes the system's climate, terrain, and suitability data.  
**2.7.2.2.3 Logical Data Flow Diagram**  
**![][image23]**  
 *Figure 2.25: Logical Data Flow Diagram*

Figure 2.25 showcases the Logical Data Flow Diagrams for the EnergyHub and EcoSim modules. In the EnergyHub, users can choose a type of renewable energy and a geographic area to pull up data on environmental factors and renewable energy suitability for visualization. Meanwhile, in EcoSim, users pick a municipality and enter details about household electricity usage. The system then gathers relevant climate and terrain information, estimates the potential energy output from solar, wind, and hydropower sources, and calculates important financial and environmental metrics. These results help users compare different renewable energy options and come up with a solid recommendation. Both modules tap into a shared database but cater to different decision-making needs.

**2.7.2.2.4 Physical Data Flow Diagram**   
**![][image24]**  
*Figure 2.26: Physical Data Flow Diagram*

Figure 2.26 presents the Physical Data Flow Diagram for the LUMI system, detailing the technical implementation of the Energy Hub and Ecosim pipelines. In the Energy Hub pipeline, the user submits a renewable type and geographic level via HTTP GET to the backend router (1.0–2.0), which checks Redis for cached suitability data (3.0) and, on a cache miss, queries the municipalities, solar\_suitability, wind\_suitability, hydropower\_suitability, and geothermal\_suitability tables (4.0), then caches and returns the choropleth map data (5.0). In the Ecosim pipeline, the user submits a municipality and household details via HTTP POST (1.0–2.0); the backend retrieves climate averages from municipality\_climate\_monthly and computes solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal output estimates using additional data from geothermal\_output and geothermal\_suitability (3.0), then calculates cost, savings, payback, and CO2 impact (4.0) before returning the comparison to the user, with an optional save to saved\_simulations (5.0). Both pipelines rely on data populated through periodic batch ETL processes that pull from external sources such as the NASA POWER API, DOE reports, Global Energy Monitor, and PHIVOLCS.

**2.7.2.2.5 Entity Relationship Diagram** 

*Figure 2.27: Entity Relationship Diagram*  
The Entity Relationship Diagram represents the logical structure of the LUMI database, showing the relationships among geographic, climate, energy, terrain, machine learning, forecasting, user tables and AI insights data tables. The database uses a normalized geographic hierarchy consisting of regions, provinces, municipalities and barangays, which enables the location-based analysis from national to municipality levels. Climate data is stored in the municipality\_climate\_monthly table, linked to municipalities and containing historical weather variables from NASA POWER(Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources), while national\_energy\_annual stores DOE-based energy statistics for forecasting, terrain-related metrics are stored in the hydropower\_suitability table, containing elevation, slope, runoff, and hydro suitability indicators. The ml\_model\_registry, forecast\_cache and chart\_ai\_insights tables manage machine learning models, forecast results and AI generated explanations.

**2.7.2.2.7 System Flow Chart**  
**![][image25]**  
*Figure 2.28: System Flowchart \- End-user*

Figure 2.28 presents the system flowchart for LUMI's authenticated user journey, beginning with the login and registration process. Upon starting the system, they arrive on the home page. Then when they go to the login page, the user is asked whether they are a new user. New users proceed to account registration, while returning users input their email and password; both paths validate the entered information and display an error message if details are missing or invalid, prompting the user to re-enter their credentials. Once authentication is successful, the session is established and the user is directed to the LUMI dashboard. From the dashboard, the user can access five main options: Home, About, Energy Hub, Ecosim, and Profile. Home and About display introductory and informational content about the system. Energy Hub allows the user to select a renewable type and geographic level, then displays regional climate data, energy intelligence, and forecasted trends. Ecosim allows the user to select a municipality and input household details such as bill, rate, and desired savings percentage, then displays a comparison between current and recommended energy options; if the user is logged in, it will automatically save their simulation into their account.The Profile option allows the user to edit their account information or log out. Selecting Logout ends the current session.

![][image26]

*Figure 2.29: System Flowchart \- Admin*

Figure 2.29 shows the system flowchart for LUMI's Admin module. When administrators log in, they enter their credentials, which are checked for authentication and role verification. Once they're successfully authenticated, authorized admins can dive into User Management, System Analytics, System Configuration, and their Profile. These features empower them to handle user accounts, analyze system usage, tweak configuration settings, and keep their account details up to date. When they're done, clicking Logout will end their active session.  
**2.7.2.2.8 Algorithm Structure**

The following section describes the core computational and machine learning algorithms implemented within LUMI. Each algorithm or formula is categorized by its domain and presented in concise paragraph form to explain its purpose, mechanism, and application within the system.

**Solar Temperature Factor Calculation**

The system adjusts photovoltaic output for deviations from the standard test condition temperature of 25 degrees Celsius. Solar panel efficiency decreases as cell temperature rises above this reference, and the temperature factor quantifies this loss as a linear function of temperature deviation (Kim et al., 2021; Zdyb & Sobczynski, 2024). Given a mean air temperature and a conservative industry-standard temperature coefficient of negative 0.004 per degree Celsius for crystalline silicon panels, the factor is computed and clamped at a minimum of zero to prevent negative power estimates. Philippine ambient temperatures frequently exceed 25 degrees Celsius in lowland municipalities, so without this correction, solar output estimates would be systematically optimistic. This factor is aggregated with other system losses within the solar performance ratio computation in the Ecosim module before daily and monthly energy output is calculated.

**Solar Performance Ratio Aggregation**

Real-world solar installations experience losses from temperature, dust accumulation, inverter inefficiency, cell mismatch, wiring resistance, and long-term degradation. The performance ratio combines these individual loss factors multiplicatively to obtain an overall system efficiency multiplier, floored at zero to prevent invalid values (Zdyb & Sobczynski, 2024). This ratio typically falls between 0.5 and 0.85 for residential installations and is the standard metric in photovoltaic engineering for translating theoretical irradiance-based output into realistic expectations, consistent with IEC 61724 guidelines. Within LUMI, dust loss and degradation loss are optionally adjusted by wind speed and humidity before aggregation, allowing the simulation to respond to local climate conditions. The result is passed to the renewable energy calculator in the Ecosim module.

**Wind Power Output Calculation**

The algorithm applies the fundamental wind power equation, which states that kinetic power in wind scales with the cube of wind speed, the swept area of the rotor, and air density (Bianchini et al., 2022). The system validates that rotor radius and wind speed are positive, air density falls within realistic bounds, and the power coefficient does not exceed the Betz limit of 0.593, the theoretical maximum aerodynamic efficiency for a horizontal-axis wind turbine (Molteno, 2022). Swept area is computed from the rotor radius, and rated power is derived by combining air density, swept area, wind speed cubed, the power coefficient, and overall mechanical-electrical efficiency. Realistic energy production accounts for variable wind conditions through a capacity factor, which addresses the critical distinction between rated power at ideal wind speed and actual energy production averaged over time, preventing the common error of assuming continuous operation at rated power. This algorithm is called by the renewable energy calculator in the Ecosim module using average rotor radius and power coefficient derived from small wind turbine product databases.

**Runoff Coefficient Estimation**

The runoff coefficient for small catchments varies with land slope because steeper terrain generates faster overland flow and less infiltration (Sambito et al., 2026). Given mean terrain slope in degrees, the coefficient is determined through piecewise classification: gentle slopes below 3 degrees representing forested or pasture land receive a coefficient of 0.30, moderate slopes between 3 and 10 degrees representing mixed land use receive 0.45, steep slopes between 10 and 20 degrees representing cultivated or hilly terrain receive 0.60, and very steep slopes above 20 degrees representing rocky or urban surfaces receive 0.75. Ungauged small catchments in the Philippines typically lack streamflow measurements, so this coefficient method, combined with monthly precipitation from NASA POWER, provides a first-order estimate of available water flow for micro-hydropower sizing. The algorithm is invoked during the hydropower design flow estimation process in the Ecosim module.

**Micro-Hydropower Design Flow Estimation**

This algorithm adapts the rational method for small catchments to estimate the design flow rate at a micro-hydropower intake. The procedure converts catchment area and monthly rainfall depth into consistent units, obtains a base runoff coefficient from the slope-based estimation algorithm, then adjusts it by terrain suitability factors including runoff potential and watershed gradient. Total monthly runoff volume is computed from the effective runoff coefficient, precipitation depth, and catchment area. Average flow is obtained by dividing the runoff volume by the total seconds in a month, and the design flow incorporates a 40 percent environmental reserve and gravity-flow feasibility before being clamped to a realistic micro-hydro intake range. The 40 percent environmental reserve follows standard practice for run-of-river systems to maintain downstream ecology, and the default catchment area represents a typical small hillside drainage accessible to a household installation (Rumbayan & Rumbayan, 2024). The algorithm is called by the renewable energy calculator in the Ecosim module using terrain metrics retrieved from the hydropower suitability table.

**Micro-Hydropower Electrical Output Calculation**

The standard hydropower equation for run-of-river micro-hydro systems computes available electrical power from design flow and hydraulic head (Di Dio et al., 2022). The flow rate is first clamped to a realistic micro-hydro range, and the hydraulic head is scaled to 12 percent of the municipal elevation range to represent the local intake-to-turbine drop accessible to a single household, bounded between 2 and 25 meters. Hydraulic power is derived from water density, gravity, flow rate, and the realistic head, then multiplied by the combined turbine and generator efficiency to obtain electrical power. Daily and monthly energy follow by scaling electrical power over time. A hydro suitability score is derived by normalizing monthly energy against a reference value for rural micro-hydro systems (Castro et al., 2023). The 12 percent head scaling reflects that only a fraction of the total municipal elevation difference is accessible to a single household intake. The algorithm is called by the renewable energy calculator in the Ecosim module after flow rate estimation.

**Economic Viability and Recommendation Scoring**

For each renewable source, the system computes economic indicators and a composite suitability score to enable the Ecosim module to recommend the best option. The algorithm first caps usable generation at actual consumption to prevent overestimation of financial benefit. Monthly savings are derived from displaced consumption and the local electricity rate. System size is estimated conservatively using a Philippine national average of 4 equivalent peak-sun hours per day, and installation cost is computed from the system size and per-kilowatt pricing. The simple payback period divides installation cost by annual savings. The energy coverage ratio compares estimated generation against consumption, and the weighted suitability score combines 60 percent energy coverage with 40 percent source quality, following the weighted linear combination approach used in GIS-MCDA renewable energy site-selection studies (Vanegas-Cantarero et al., 2022). Carbon displacement is computed using the DOE 2019-2021 National Grid Emission Factor. The simple payback period is the dominant first-screening metric in residential photovoltaic techno-economic studies (Ngwakwe, 2025). This algorithm is called for each of solar, wind, and hydro options, then aggregated to select the highest-scoring recommendation in the Ecosim dashboard response builder.

**ARIMA Time-Series Forecasting**

An AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average model with order one-one-one projects future national energy consumption and peak demand using historical annual data. The model captures trend and short-term autocorrelation in the first-differenced series, where the original time-series of consumption or peak demand is differenced once to remove non-stationarity, and the resulting series is modeled as a combination of an autoregressive term, a moving average term, and white noise. The model was trained offline using the statsmodels library with maximum likelihood estimation on Philippine national energy statistics from 2003 to 2020\. Forecasts for 2025 to 2030 were generated with 95 percent confidence intervals and exported to comma-separated value artifacts. ARIMA provides a strong statistical baseline for national-level time-series forecasting; its interpretability and requirement for only the target variable, without exogenous predictors, make it suitable when macroeconomic drivers are not available at sufficient temporal resolution (Markovics & Mayer, 2022). The artifacts are loaded at runtime by the machine learning prediction service and served through the EnergyHub service.

**Composite Renewable Potential Score for Choropleth Mapping**

To support the provincial choropleth map in the EnergyHub dashboard, the system aggregates municipal climate and terrain data into a single renewable potential score. For each province, average solar irradiance, average wind speed, and average hydropower suitability are combined using weighted linear combination. Each component is normalized against its theoretical maximum, then weighted and summed: solar receives the largest weight at 40 percent, while wind and hydropower each receive 30 percent. The resulting composite score is scaled to a 0 to 100 range and rounded to two decimal places. The weighting reflects that solar irradiance is the most spatially variable and readily exploitable resource at the residential scale in the Philippines, while wind and hydropower contributions vary more strongly by local geography. This score enables intuitive choropleth mapping while reflecting the multi-source nature of renewable energy potential (Candan et al., 2022). It is computed within the renewable potential map builder in the EnergyHub service.

**2.7.2.2.9 AI Tools and APIs**

The study used a number of AI libraries and API to enable the functionality of the system. The primary AI used is the Gemini 2.5 Flash from Google which serves as the primary Large language model (LLM) utilized in the system, while Groq serves as the backup LLM. The Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) has been used for vector similarity search, a machine learning technique that uses context to learn concepts. Meanwhile, HuggingFace all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a sentence transformer that has been used for text embeddings in the system.

**2.7.3 Testing Procedures**   
**2.7.3.1 System Test Plan (all Interfaces and process testing and results)** 

The system test plan has been created to test the functionality and features of the system. It includes a series of structured test cases designed to ensure that all integrated components operate as intended under expected conditions. The test plan covers areas such as user authentication, module access, feature responsiveness, data handling and role-based permissions.

| Aspect | Description |
| ----- | ----- |
| Objective | Stress tests the system to ensure robustness under multitasking conditions. Test all modules significant for forecasting accuracy, AI assistant quality, Ecosim calculation correctness, terrain pipeline integrity, and visualization performance. Ensure the system is ready before releasing it to users. |
| Test Scope | The test covers core functionalities of the environmental intelligence platform, including user interface, data processing pipelines, machine learning forecasting modules, Ecosim renewable energy calculations, terrain analysis pipeline, AI assistant integration, and performance under normal usage. |
| Testing Approach | The testing environment consists of the researchers’ personal laptops and desktop computers, each configured to simulate various user conditions. The system is deployed across multiple devices to observe its behavior in different operating systems, browsers, and screen resolutions. This setup allows for a controlled yet diverse testing scenario, ensuring that the platform’s performance remains stable and consistent across different hardware and software environments. |
| Test Environment | The testing is conducted internally by the researchers, using individual accounts to simulate multiple user experiences. Each researcher performs repeated testing cycles to evaluate the system’s responsiveness, reliability, and overall functionality. **2.7.4 Deployment**

The system is deployed as a web-based system that can be accessed on any device with a web browser and an internet connection. This increases compatibility and allows the system to be used without installing it first on device. Therefore, this ensures that the system is available for all supported web browsers without requiring separate software installations for different platforms. 

**2.8 Testing and Evaluation** 

This section presents the comprehensive testing and evaluation plan for LUMI. This includes the documentation of the objectives, approaches, procedures, test cases, metrics and evaluation criteria. All of the tests are designed to validate functional correctness, computational accuracy, usability, system integration and software quality according to internationally recognized standards.

**2.8.1 Unit testing**

Unit testing was performed during the development phase to verify the correctness of individual components and modules of the system. This includes testing specific functions such as user authentication, renewable energy calculations, forecast data retrieval, Ecosim simulation triggers, and AI assistant query handling. The goal is to detect and resolve errors early before deploying the system as a whole.

For the renewable energy calculation modules, unit tests were written to validate the solar temperature factor, performance ratio aggregation, wind power output, runoff coefficient estimation, micro-hydropower design flow, and economic viability scoring. Each test supplies climate and terrain inputs representing Philippine municipal conditions and asserts that the returned values fall within physically plausible ranges.

Frontend components were tested using the React Testing Library with Vitest to verify that dashboard charts render correctly, form validations trigger appropriately, and navigation flows behave as expected. Backend API endpoints were tested using pytest with HTTPX to confirm that authentication, forecast retrieval, Ecosim submission, and AI assistant interactions return the correct status codes and response structures.

**2.8.2 Usability testing**

The final usability evaluation involved 100 household end users from Region IV-A (CALABARZON). Geographic quotas were used to include 20 participants each from Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, and Quezon. Participants were recruited based on their eligibility as members of LUMI's intended household user group. The equal allocation ensured that all five CALABARZON provinces contributed to the final system evaluation.

During the usability evaluation, participants interacted with LUMI's key features, such as the EnergyHub dashboard, EcoSim simulations, renewable energy suggestions, and AI-powered tools. Once they had a chance to explore the system, they filled out a structured questionnaire that included 12 usability statements. These statements focused on aspects like how clear the interface was, how easy it was to navigate, how well they could complete tasks, and their overall experience with usability. Additionally, there were seven more statements that asked them to compare their experience with LUMI to their usual methods of evaluating renewable energy options. All of these statements were rated on a five-point Likert scale.

**2.8.3 System testing**

System testing involved checking the entire platform as a whole to ensure that all modules work together as intended. This includes validating integrations between the React frontend interface, FastAPI backend services, machine learning prediction pipeline, and Supabase PostgreSQL database. It also covered performance under various conditions, such as concurrent user load and diverse input variety.

End-to-end scenarios were executed to verify complete user workflows: from registration and login, through EnergyHub dashboard loading and forecast visualization, to Ecosim simulation submission and result interpretation. Integration tests confirmed that frontend requests to backend endpoints returned valid JSON within acceptable response times, that database queries resolved foreign key relationships correctly, and that the ML predictor loaded pre-computed forecast artifacts without errors.

Performance testing was conducted to evaluate the system's behavior under stress. Scenarios included rendering historical trend charts with twenty years of multi-series data, submitting concurrent Ecosim requests for multiple municipalities, and measuring API response times under simulated load. 

**2.8.4 Pilot run**

The pilot run was conducted prior to formal evaluation to gather direct feedback and open-ended suggestions from actual users. This early phase focused on collecting insights that would guide improvements to both the platform's design and recommendation content before any major testing or implementation. The goal was to ensure that the development remained aligned with user expectations and needs.

Participants included household decision-makers from CALABARZON, barangay officials from selected reference provinces, licensed electrical and electronics engineers. They were asked to freely explore the LUMI platform, interact with its EnergyHub dashboard, execute Ecosim simulations for their home municipalities, and converse with the AI assistant. They then provided detailed feedback on areas such as clarity of visualizations, navigation intuitiveness, recommendation usefulness, and overall experience.

By placing emphasis on user suggestions and improvement-oriented feedback, the pilot run served as a foundation for refining the platform prior to structured evaluation phases such as usability assessments, ISO 25010 questionnaire administration, and expert validation interviews. Observations from the pilot deployment were recorded to identify final areas for refinement before the system was considered ready for broader use.

**2.8.5 Evaluation rubrics (ISO 25010 Questionnaire)**

The study utilized three complementary evaluation instruments to assess the developed LUMI system from user-centered, software-quality, and domain-specific technical perspectives. The first instrument was a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire administered to household end users from Region IV-A and focused on the usability of the system, including clarity, learnability, navigation, ease of task completion, and overall ease of use. A separate set of items also assessed how LUMI compared with the respondents' usual or conventional methods of evaluating renewable-energy options. The second instrument was given to IT experts and focused on eight specific software product quality characteristics outlined in ISO/IEC 25010:2023. These characteristics include functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, and safety. Experts evaluated these traits using a five-point rating scale, and there was also a Not Applicable (N/A) option for any items that couldn’t be reasonably assessed. The third instrument was administered to engineering experts to evaluate the technical plausibility of LUMI's renewable-energy recommendations. In addition to evaluating relevant system characteristics, each engineer independently identified the most appropriate renewable-energy source for selected locations. These independent recommendations were compared with the recommendations generated by LUMI to determine the system's agreement rate with engineering expert judgment. Using three separate evaluator groups allowed the study to distinguish between end-user experience, software product quality, and renewable-energy domain validity rather than requiring a single respondent group to evaluate all aspects of the system. The results helped identify the system’s strengths and areas for improvement, guiding further refinements to align the platform with global benchmarks of software excellence.

**2.9 Ethical Considerations**

**2.9.1 Informed consent**

Prior to data collection, we made sure to inform participants about the study's purpose, their rights, and how we would keep their information confidential. We also provided them with the right contact details for any research-related questions. In the household and IT expert evaluation questionnaires, there was a consent statement where respondents could show their willingness to participate. We emphasized that joining the study was completely voluntary and that their answers would be used solely for academic purposes. Additionally, barangay officials and engineering field experts were briefed on the study's goals and invited to take part through the proper consent procedures.

**2.9.2 Data privacy**

Respondent data was treated as confidential rather than anonymous, as the survey allowed but did not require respondents to provide their name. Respondents retained the right to withdraw their consent and request the removal of their data at any point prior to final data analysis.

**2.9.3 Confidentiality**

Collected data was handled with strict confidentiality throughout the research process. Raw responses, including any identifying information provided, were accessible only to the researchers and were permanently deleted once the dataset had been de-identified for analysis. Processed, de-identified data is stored in an encrypted file folder accessible only to the research team.

**2.9.4 Conflict of Interest**

The researchers declare that they have no conflicts of interest related to the conduct of this study.

**2.10 Research Instruments Used** 

**2.10.1 Content Validation**

The research instruments used in this study were validated by three content validators: a faculty member, a faculty member who also serves as an IT consultant, and a Principal Consultant (Software Quality Analyst) at Oracle Philippines Corporation. Each validator was provided with a quantitative and qualitative validation tool, corresponding to the relevant research instrument, and their feedback was used to refine the instruments prior to data collection. 

**2.10.2 Expert Validators**

During the initial data-gathering phase, the researchers consulted with four field experts in Electrical Engineering (EE) and Electronics and Communications Engineering (ECE). Two of them were interviewed in real-time, while the other two shared their insights asynchronously. Their valuable perspectives on renewable-energy systems, data reliability, infrastructure, and decision-support methods played a crucial role in fine-tuning LUMI's technical criteria and overall system design.

Prior to the household end-user evaluation, the researchers consulted with ten IT specialists. These experts, each with a focus on areas like software development, data analytics, IT support, IT education, software quality assurance, and project consulting, took a close look at LUMI's software quality. They based their assessment on eight specific characteristics outlined in ISO/IEC 25010:2023.

Additionally, five EE and ECE experts participated for the final technical evaluation. They thoroughly examined LUMI's functionality and its renewable-energy recommendations. Their independent recommendations were then compared with LUMI’s generated results to determine the level of agreement with professional engineering judgement. 

**2.10.3 Expert Consultation**

In addition to instrument and technical validation, the researchers consulted with their technical adviser and thesis professor throughout the study. Their feedback and guidance contributed to the development and refinement of the research design and the system's technical design.

**2.10.4 Survey Questionnaire**

The preliminary survey questionnaire was administered to 196 household decision-makers in Region IV-A (CALABARZON). This survey featured a mix of structured questions, such as multiple-response checkboxes, yes-or-no queries, five-point rating scales, and a six-point scale to gauge renewable energy knowledge. Through this questionnaire valuable insights  were gathered into the respondents' concerns about electricity, their awareness of renewable energy, system requirements, and personal preferences. The results provided a solid foundation for understanding user needs and shaping the development of LUMI.

**2.10.5 End-User System Evaluation Questionnaire**

The end-user evaluation questionnaire was administered with 100 household respondents who had the chance to use LUMI. This questionnaire consisted of 12 usability statements inspired by Nielsen's usability principles, focusing on aspects like ease of use, understandability, navigation, interface organization, task completion, and error guidance. An additional seven statements assessed the respondents perceived experience with LUMI compared to their usual methods for evaluating renewable energy options. All of these statements were evaluated on a five-point Likert scale.

**2.10.6 IT Expert Software Quality Evaluation Questionnaire** 

The IT expert questionnaire was administered to ten IT professionals to evaluate LUMI's technical software quality. This evaluation was based on eight key characteristics from the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 framework: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, and safety. To make the process straightforward, we used a five-point rating scale, including a Not Applicable (N/A) option for any items that couldn't be assessed through testing, observation, or the technical documentation.

**2.10.7 Engineering Recommendation Validation Form** 

The engineering validation instrument was administered to five engineering field experts to evaluate LUMI's technical performance and its suggestions for renewable energy. This instrument included a series of technical evaluation questions and an independent recommendation section. In this section, the experts chose from options like Solar, Wind, Hydropower, Geothermal, or Insufficient Information for each location they assessed. Their recommendations were compared with the results generated by LUMI to determine the frequency and percentage of agreement.

**2.11 Statistical Treatment of Data** 

**2.11.1 Statistical Design**

The IT expert evaluation focused on eight specific software product quality characteristics as outlined in ISO/IEC 25010:2023. Each characteristic was examined through evaluation statements that pertained to LUMI's technical functionality and performance. To gather insights, a questionnaire featuring a five-point rating scale was utilized, including a Not Applicable (N/A) option for items that couldn't be reasonably assessed. The quality characteristics that were evaluated include:

**Functional Suitability**

Evaluates how effectively LUMI carries out its intended functions, such as account registration and authentication, visualizing energy data, providing recommendations for renewable energy, forecasting, and running EcoSim simulations. It also examines whether the different modules of the system work together seamlessly to enhance the overall renewable energy evaluation process.

**Performance Efficiency**

Assesses LUMI's response times, how well it uses resources, and its overall processing power. It includes aspects like page loading speeds, the efficiency of recommendation and simulation processing, responses from the AI assistant, as well as CPU and memory usage. Additionally, it examines network resource management and performance when handling anticipated workloads from multiple users and transactions.

**Compatibility**

Evaluates the ability of LUMI to exchange information with external data sources and services. It assesses whether the system can consistently fetch, process, and incorporate the external information it needs to perform its intended tasks effectively.

**Reliability**

Assesses LUMI's stability during normal operation, checking how well it keeps its functions intact even when there are component or service failures, and how effectively it can bounce back from any system interruptions that have been tested.

**Security**

Evaluates LUMI's protection of user information and system operations from unauthorized access or alterations. It includes a review of authentication processes, authorization measures, security logging practices, and how the system deals with invalid inputs and attempts at unauthorized access.

**Maintainability**

Assesses how effectively LUMI's software components can be modified or upgraded without causing disruptions to other functions. The emphasis is on keeping components separate, ensuring modularity, and making it easy to implement changes.

**Flexibility**

Evaluates LUMI's ability to adapt to changes in supported technical environments it supports and handle growing processing needs. It takes into account the system's flexibility and its potential to scale up as operational demands evolve.

**Safety**

Assesses LUMI's ability to identify incomplete or unavailable information that might impact the trustworthiness of its results. It also checks if the system gives suitable alerts when its recommendations come with uncertainties that users need to keep in mind.

**2.11.2 Statistical Method** 

Different statistical methods were applied according to the purpose and type of data gathered during the preliminary requirements-gathering and final system-evaluation phases. For the preliminary needs-analysis survey involving household decision-makers, frequency and percentage distributions were used to summarize categorical, multiple-response, and yes-or-no items. Weighted mean was used to determine the central tendency of responses to Likert-scale and ordinal items concerning renewable-energy concerns, user requirements, preferences, and likelihood of adoption.

For the final household end-user evaluation,  weighted mean and standard deviation were used to summarize respondents' assessments about LUMI's usability and its ability to support decision-making. Cronbach's alpha was employed to assess the internal consistency of our 12-item usability scale and the seven-item scale that compares it to previous methods.

To test the hypothesis of the study, a one-sample right-tailed t-test was applied to the respondent-level composite scores derived from the seven comparison-with-prior-methods items. The neutral midpoint of 3.00 on the five-point evaluation scale was used as the hypothesized population mean, with a significance level of 0.05. The test determined whether the average comparison score was significantly greater than the neutral benchmark. A statistically significant result would support the conclusion that participating respondents perceived LUMI as providing better support for household renewable-energy evaluation and decision-making than their usual or conventional methods. However, the findings would represent perceived improvement rather than an experimentally established improvement in actual decision-making performance.

For the IT expert evaluation, weighted mean and standard deviation were used to summarize the experts' assessments of the applicable ISO/IEC 25010 software product quality characteristics. The weighted mean represented the overall evaluation of each quality characteristic, while standard deviation indicated the variability of the experts' assessments. The responses marked as Not Applicable (N/A) were excluded from the numerical calculations, and only valid ratings were considered when computing for the weighted mean and standard deviation. 

For the engineering expert evaluation, weighted mean and standard deviation were used to summarize their technical assessments of LUMI. Percentage agreement was also employed to determine the correspondence between LUMI's generated renewable-energy recommendations and the independent recommendations provided by engineering experts for selected Philippine locations. Responses indicating "Insufficient Information" were excluded from the denominator when an expert could not provide a valid renewable-energy recommendation. The number of matching recommendations and corresponding agreement rate were reported together to ensure transparency. When all five engineering evaluators provided valid recommendations, four matching recommendations corresponded to an agreement rate of 80%, while five matching recommendations indicated unanimous agreement.

For the predictive component of LUMI, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) were used to evaluate forecasting performance. MAE measured the average absolute difference between predicted and actual values, while RMSE assigned greater weight to larger prediction errors. Lower MAE and RMSE values indicated better forecasting performance. System response-time measurements were also recorded to assess the performance efficiency of LUMI during system testing.

**Percentage**

Percentage was used to determine the proportion of respondents who selected a particular answer or belonged to a specific category. It was applied to the preliminary needs-analysis survey to summarize demographic characteristics, household energy concerns, renewable-energy preferences, and other categorical responses.

![][image27]

*Where:*  
P \= Percentage  
f \= Frequency of responses for a given category  
n \= Total number of respondents

**Weighted Mean**

Weighted mean was utilized to determine the average assessment of respondents and evaluators based on their selected rating-scale values. It was applied to the preliminary needs-analysis survey and the final household, IT expert, and engineering expert evaluations to summarize responses concerning system requirements, usability, software quality, and technical suitability.

**![][image28]**

*Where:*  
x̄w \= Weighted mean  
fᵢ \= Frequency (number of respondents who selected a given scale value)  
xᵢ \= Scale value  
n \= Total number of responses to the item

**Standard Deviation**

Standard deviation was employed to measure the dispersion of respondents' ratings around their mean. It was used to assess the variability of household usability and comparison ratings, as well as IT and engineering expert evaluations. A lower standard deviation indicated that ratings were more closely clustered around the mean, while a higher standard deviation indicated greater variation among responses.

![][image29]  
*Where:*  
σ \= Standard deviation   
fᵢ \= Frequency (number of respondents or evaluators who selected a given scale value)  
xᵢ \= Scale value  
x̄ \= Mean or weighted mean of the evaluated item  
n \= total number of respondents 

**Cronbach's Alpha**

Cronbach's alpha was utilized to assess the internal consistency reliability of the household usability and comparison-with-prior-methods questionnaires. The analysis covered the 12-item usability scale and the seven-item comparison scale to determine the degree to which the items within each instrument consistently measured their intended constructs. Higher Cronbach's alpha values generally indicate stronger internal consistency, although the coefficient alone does not establish the validity of the questionnaire (Tavakol & Dennick, 2011).

**![][image30]**  
*Where:*

k \= Total number of questionnaire items within the scale  
Σ \= Summation symbol  
sᵢ² \= Variance of scores for each questionnaire item  
sₜ² \= Variance of the total questionnaire scores

**One-Sample Right-Tailed t-Test**

A one-sample right-tailed t-test was employed to determine whether the mean comparison-with-prior-methods score of the household respondents was significantly greater than the neutral midpoint of 3.00 on the five-point evaluation scale. The test was applied to respondent-level composite scores using a significance level of 0.05. A statistically significant result would indicate that participating respondents perceived LUMI as providing better support for household renewable-energy evaluation and decision-making compared with their usual or conventional methods. However, the findings would reflect perceived improvement rather than an experimentally established improvement in decision-making performance.

**![][image31]**  
**Where:**

s \= Sample standard deviation of the respondent-level composite scores  
n \= Number of valid respondents

The hypothesis was evaluated using a significance level of 0.05. The null hypothesis was rejected when the computed right-tailed p-value was less than 0.05; otherwise, the null hypothesis was not rejected. The statistical findings were interpreted in relation to the respondents' mean ratings, standard deviations, and the limitations of the non-probability sampling design.

**CHAPTER 3**  
**RESULTS AND DISCUSSION**  
This chapter presents the results and discussion of LUMI system's development, testing, and evaluation. Including the project description, system structure, graphical user interface, and findings from the household end-user, IT expert, and engineering expert evaluations. The results are analyzed and interpreted in relation to the study's objectives and the effectiveness of LUMI as a renewable-energy decision-support system. 

**3.1 Project Description** 

LUMI, is a web-based renewable energy source recommendation and decision support system. It is created as a tool to enable end users to determine various renewable energy options available to them, provide recommendations, and allow them to make informed, data-driven decisions related to implementing renewable energy systems to their intended application. To achieve its purpose as a recommendation and decision support system, LUMI have the following modules: 

* **Ecosim module,** provides the comparison between existing and available renewable energy options.

* **Energy Hub module,** provides the regional data such as climate data, energy data, geographical data, and forecasted energy demand and consumption.

* **Multi-criteria decision making (MCDM) module,** serves as the core engine of the system for environmental intelligence, determines the suitability of the renewable energy source, and generates the appropriate recommendations.

**3.4  Analysis of Data**

The final evaluation of LUMI took place through online questionnaires filled out by 115 participants. This group included 100 household end-users from Region IV-A (CALABARZON), along with ten IT experts and five engineering specialists. The household respondents were chosen using geographic quota sampling, ensuring that there were 20 participants from each province in CALABARZON. They provided feedback on the system's usability and its perceived ability to support decision-making. Meanwhile, the IT and engineering professionals focused on assessing the software quality, technical performance, and recommendations related to renewable energy.

In the following tables, you'll find the results from the household usability evaluations and comparisons with previous methods, as well as the IT expert assessments based on eight selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 software product quality characteristics. Additionally, the evaluations from the engineering experts are included. These findings were carefully analyzed to gauge LUMI's perceived usability, software quality, technical performance, and how well they aligned with independent engineering recommendations.

Table 3.1 presents the criteria used to interpret the weighted mean scores from the household usability evaluation, IT expert software quality evaluation, and engineering technical evaluation of LUMI. The same five-level interpretation scale was applied to the numerical ratings of all three respondent groups to maintain consistency in presenting and interpreting the evaluation results.

**3.6  Functionality Evaluation**

The functionality of LUMI was assessed through system testing and the functional suitability evaluation conducted by ten IT experts. The assessment covered account registration and authentication, EnergyHub data visualization, renewable-energy recommendations, energy-demand forecasting, EcoSim simulations, and the integration of the system's modules.

The evaluation obtained an overall weighted mean of 4.40 and a standard deviation of 0.61, interpreted as Excellent based on the established evaluation criteria. These findings indicate that the IT experts positively assessed LUMI's ability to perform its intended functions and support preliminary renewable-energy decision-making.

**3.7  ISO 25010 Software Evaluation Tool**

The software quality of LUMI was evaluated by ten IT experts using a questionnaire based on eight selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 software product quality characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, and safety. The experts assessed the system through applicable evaluation statements using a five-point rating scale. The results were analyzed using weighted mean and standard deviation to determine the overall assessment of each quality characteristic.

**3.8 Acceptability Survey (User Acceptability Test )**

The acceptability of LUMI among household end-users was assessed using the usability evaluation and comparison-with-prior-methods questionnaire administered to 100 respondents from the CALABARZON region. The questionnaire consisted of 12 usability statements based on Nielsen's usability principles and seven statements assessing respondents' perceived experience with LUMI compared with their usual methods of evaluating renewable-energy options.

The usability evaluation obtained an overall weighted mean of 4.73 and a standard deviation of 0.38, interpreted as Excellent. Meanwhile, the comparison-with-prior-methods evaluation obtained an overall weighted mean of 4.79 and a standard deviation of 0.32, also interpreted as Excellent.

These results indicate that household respondents positively assessed LUMI's ease of use, clarity, navigation, and perceived decision-support capabilities. The findings suggest a high level of user acceptability among the participating households, particularly in supporting preliminary renewable-energy evaluation and decision-making.

**3.9 Interpretation of Data**

The study results show that LUMI was liked by household end users and IT experts. Engineering experts said that LUMI still needs some improvement. These results give a picture of how usable LUMI is, how well it supports decisions, how good the software is, how suitable the technology is and how well LUMI matches professional recommendations.

Household users said they usually ask family, friends or look online when choosing energy. Table 3.2 shows that 65 percent talked to family or friends and 59 percent searched the internet. These results show that it is useful to give households a platform that brings together renewable energy information and helps them make early decisions. For usability LUMI scored a mean of 4.73 with a variation of 0.38, which is excellent. LUMI was also compared with methods and received a weighted mean of 4.79 and a variation of 0.32, also excellent. These scores show that household users found LUMI easy to use and thought it gave information and better help than their normal ways.

The reliability test shows that LUMI’s usability score had a Cronbach alpha of 0.923 and the comparison with methods had a Cronbach alpha of 0.868. This means the scores are very consistent. A one-sample tailed t-test gave a t-value of 55.47 and a p-value less than 0.001. Because this p-value is below 0.05 the test rejects the hypothesis. That means respondents rated LUMI higher than the score of 3.00. These results only show how users feel, not how LUMI actually performs compared to a pretest and posttest.

IT experts gave LUMI scores for all eight ISO/IEC 25010:2023 software quality criteria. LUMI’s weighted mean was 4.46 with a variation of 0.60, which is excellent. The top score was for compatibility at 4.65. Then maintainability was 4.60 and safety was 4.50. Flexibility had the score at 4.20, which is very good. These results show that IT experts liked LUMI for its function, speed, ability to work with systems, ease of maintenance and other quality measures. They also said that LUMI could still be better in flexibility.

Engineering experts gave LUMI a score. The overall weighted mean was 3.27 with a variation of 0.18, which's satisfactory. Suitability and interaction capability each scored 3.40. Reliability and safety scored 3.00. These scores show that LUMI is okay for renewable‑energy checks but the lower engineering scores mean that LUMI still needs improvement in how technically sound its recommendations are, how it shows supporting data and how it explains the uncertainties and limits.

The expert recommendation check gave an agreement of 82.22 percent meaning 37 out of 45 valid expert‑location matches were the same. This is higher than the 80 percent minimum that the study set. Agreement was not the same for all nine places; Bulacan and Cavite each had 60 percent. These results show that LUMI’s suggestions match the experts in cases but some locations still need more work. The agreement shows how well LUMI matches expert advice, not how accurate LUMI really is.

The performance test also showed how LUMI works technically. Forecast tests measured Mean Absolute Error and Root Mean Squared Error showing that LUMI’s predictions differ from energy values. This means uncertainty in forecasting is still an issue. The system also had an API response time of about 104 milliseconds in local tests. A full EcoSim run with an AI recommendation took 612 milliseconds. These times are good under the tested conditions. They may change if the network or workload is different.

Overall the results show that LUMI is a web tool for early household renewable‑energy checks. LUMI did best in how easy it was to use for households, how it seemed to help decision making and how good the software's.. The lower scores from engineering experts and the mixed agreement with experts mean that LUMI still needs more work on its technical checks, how it gives recommendations and how it shows uncertainty. So LUMI is best used as a first‑step decision aid that works alongside engineering reviews not as a replacement.

*Table 3.4: Comparison with Prior Methods*

Table 3.4 shows how household end-users rated LUMI when compared to their ways of assessing renewable-energy options. The overall weighted mean score was 4.79 with a deviation of 0.32. This result is interpreted as Excellent. Out of the seven statements the weighted mean was 4.88. This means that users strongly agreed that LUMI gives support for evaluating and deciding on renewable energy than their usual methods. The weighted mean was 4.70, which relates to how easy it is to compare different renewable-energy options. Still even the lowest score was considered Excellent. These results show that users saw LUMI as a decision-support tool. It gives information, makes comparisons simpler and reduces the effort needed for initial evaluations. However these findings are based on user perceptions. They do not reflect objective improvements in how well people perform tasks.
