*Table 3.19: Expert Recommendation Validation*  
Table 3.18 presents the agreement of LUMI’s renewable-energy recommendation with the five expert evaluators’ recommendations at the nine locations. Out of the 45 expert evaluations that were valid for analysis, 37 were in agreement with LUMI’s recommendations, which resulted in an 82.22% overall agreement. For this study, the overall agreement threshold that was considered for an 80% minimum was used as a basis. This threshold was justified by expert-consensus literature as 80% agreement was conceptualized as the level of consensus by Hohmann et al. (2025). Meanwhile, Škrinjar et al. (2026) in a meta-research study on 1,904 Delphi studies identified 80% as the most common percentage-based consensus threshold cited in the studies.

As LUMI’s overall agreement of 82.22% was above the established overall agreement threshold of 80%, the result was interpreted as an acceptable agreement between LUMI’s and the expert evaluators’ recommendations. In the location level, Camarines Sur, Leyte, and Batangas achieved 100% agreement, while Eastern Samar, Laguna, Rizal, and Quezon achieved 80% agreement. Agreement was the lowest in Bulacan and Cavite with 60% agreement.

The level of agreement at the location level was used only as a basis to determine whether LUMI’s recommendations were more or less consistent with the recommendations of the expert evaluators. It was the overall level of agreement of 82.22% that was the main consideration for evaluating the level of agreement of LUMI’s recommendations with the expert evaluations. The 80% threshold for the level of overall agreement was used only as a methodological reference and not as a software standard because the present study did not make use of the Delphi method.

**Overall Agreement Rate Interpretation Criteria**

| Agreement Rate | Interpretation |
| :---: | :---: |
| 100% | Unanimous Agreement |
| 90% \- 99.99%  | Very High Agreement |
| 80% \- 89.99% | Acceptable Agreement |
| 70%-79.99% | Moderate Agreement / Needs Review |
| Below 70% | Low Agreement / Requires Refinement |

*Table 3.20: Overall Agreement Rate Interpretation Criteria*  
Table 3.20 represents the criteria on which the overall agreement rate between LUMI’s overall agreement rate and the expert recommendations in each location will be interpreted. If the software demonstrates an overall agreement rate between 90% and 100%, it is interpreted as a Very High Agreement, while an overall agreement rate between 80% and 89.99% means Acceptable Agreement. An overall agreement rate (OAR) between 70% and 79.99% indicates Moderate Agreement / Needs Review, while an OAR below 70% indicates Low Agreement / Requires Refinement. However, for this research, an agreement rate of at least 80% was considered acceptable.

**![][image45]**  
*Figure 3.20: Agreement Rate Between LUMI and Expert Recommendations by Location*  
The agreement rate between LUMI and the expert recommendations varied for the nine locations. Camarines Sur, Leyte, and Batangas acquired 100%, indicating that the software recommendation was completely agreed upon by the experts. Eastern Samar, Laguna, Rizal, and Quezon garnered 80%, which was the minimum needed for an acceptable agreement. Lastly, Bulacan and Cavite only scored 60%, which was below the minimum needed for an acceptable agreement. The results can be said to be generally positive as seven locations got an acceptable or complete agreement. This implies that most recommendations made by the software were similar to those of the experts.  
**LUMI System Performance Metrics**

| Performance Metric | Result | Interpretation |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| MAE | ARIMA(1,1,1) forecasts deviated by an average of 6,829.09 GWh/yr on national consumption (≈5.7% of the \~120 TWh annual figure), 1,019.66 MW on peak demand (≈5.6%), and 3,597.39 GWh/yr on renewable generation (≈13.7%) across the held-out 2021–2024 test years — comparable to or better than all five baseline models in the same evaluation run. | The model manages to reach a single-digit percentage error against both of the headline targets, well below the benchmark of 18% MAPE not hit by Philippine demand forecasting studies referenced in our literature review, considering that it is a first-generation model trained on only 18 yearly observations. Renewable generation, the hardest target to forecast, is the result of RE output; the reason is high volatility of the data provided, and this issue will be resolved with our scheduled changes in the data used. |
| RMSE | RMSE values of 8,257.12 GWh (consumption), 1,299.08 MW (peak demand), and 3,939.69 GWh (renewable generation) — each roughly 20–30% higher than its corresponding MAE, indicating errors were concentrated in a single year rather than spread evenly. | The difference between the RMSE and MAE shows that the model generally followed the trend throughout most years but failed to predict the demand at the national level in 2024, when it suddenly increased beyond the trend suggested by the training data from 2003 to 2020\. The various candidate models all exhibited this under-forecast, which means the problem lay in the abrupt change in the rate of demand growth and not in the choice of model. |
| ART | The system responded in \~104 ms on average across 21 measured API endpoints (30 runs each for standard endpoints, 5 for compute-heavy flows): standard endpoints averaged \~49 ms — most under 10 ms — while the heaviest user flow, a full EcoSim simulation with AI recommendation, completed in \~612 ms. | The levels of response time remain well under the predetermined limits—API below 2,000 ms, AI below 5,000 ms, and web page loads below 3,000 ms—entitling the system to an Excellent rating in terms of its performance regarding time. Indeed, the slowest response recorded is about eight times below its limit and results in an average response time of less than 50 ms per request, so that both the dashboards, the maps, and the suggestions appear almost instantaneous to users. The two auth-gated endpoints are excluded from the total, which is why the figures reflect the actual time taken to handle requests. The values are based on a local benchmark, and since the latency that has been implemented also varies with network conditions, there is still some room for making adjustments. |

*Note. ART \- Average Response Time, MAE \- Mean Absolute Error, RMSE \- Root Mean Squared Error*

**3.4 interpretation of Data** 

**CHAPTER 4**  
**SUMMARY, CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS**  
This chapter covers the summary of the results and discussion of the study. It covers the discussion of the project description, structure, user interface design, system planning, survey results, and result analysis of the study. These provide the context to the objectives achieved by the study.  
**4.1 Summary of Findings**  
**4.1.1 Household Respondents**  
Household respondents determined that the system is highly usable and provides comprehensive decision support for determining the appropriate renewable energy source. Prior to using LUMI, most respondents rely on asking people they know, searching information online, or manually comparing each option themselves to determine which renewable energy they should use.   
**4.1.2 IT Experts**  
IT Experts evaluated the system to be very good based on the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality evaluation framework.  The system is deemed sufficient to meet the ISO/IEC 25010 standards for functional suitability, performance efficiency,  compatibility, reliability, maintainability, flexibility, and safety. This makes LUMI fit for use as renewable energy decision support in the software quality perspective.  
**4.1.3 Engineering Experts**   
The results of the evaluation conducted by engineering experts indicate that the LUMI performed satisfactorily. LUMI gained satisfactory remarks in functional suitability, interaction capability, and reliability and safety. The recommendations given by the system had an 82.22% overall match with recommendations from engineering experts, which indicates acceptable agreement between the LUMI and the engineers.  
The evaluations conducted by the study indicates that system has an overall very good performance across all three respondent types. Household gave LUMI an overall score of 4.79 out of 5 with a standard deviation of 0.32, which indicates an excellent rating for usability. The ISO/IEC 25010 software product quality assessment conducted by IT Experts yielded a score of 4.46 out of 5 and a standard deviation of 0.60. This indicates that LUMI has been evaluated to be a excellent software based on ISO standards. Lastly, field expert engineers gave LUMI a score of 3.27 out of 5 with a standard deviation of 0.26, which indicates satisfactory performance for field experts. Overall, the system has been evaluated to be very good.  
**4.2 Conclusion**   
**4.2.1** The study successfully develops LUMI into a web-based decision support system that can help identify the appropriate renewable energy source for various household environments. The system has been able to be developed with weighted multi-criteria recommendation engine to identify suitable renewable energy sources. Other features such as predictive analytics module for forecasting energy demand trends and interactive map-based interface has also been implemented in the system.  
**4.2.2** The system is indicated to be usable and user-friendly as indicated by the results of the surveys conducted to household users. Meanwhile, the system is considered very good after being evaluated using the ISO/IEC 25010 software evaluation standard by IT Experts. Overall, the system is excellent as a software as evaluated by both household users and IT Experts.  
**4.2.3** The recommendation provided by LUMI on evaluated provinces in Region IV-A CALABARZON is an 82.22% match with field expert recommendations. This shows that LUMI delivers an acceptable match to expert recommendations and therefore indicate that it is capable of providing recommendations that is comparable to a field expert engineer in renewable energy sources.

As indicated by evaluations conducted by household users, IT Experts, and field expert engineers, there is an substantiation that LUMI is user-friendly, meets software quality standards established by ISO, and generate recommendations that is analogous to field experts. Therefore, LUMI has been successfully developed as a decision support system designed for household use to provide renewable energy source recommendations.

**4.3 Implementation Plan**  
Since the early conceptual phase of LUMI, it has already been intended to be a web-based online system. This approach has been chosen to ensure the widest possible compatibility while only needing to create a single software. Meanwhile, most of the processing happens in the back end of the system to minimize resources needed on end devices.   
There are plans on using LUMI as a start-up and offer a subscription based payment model for using the system with an option for a one-time payment for single use operations. Widening the scope of users to include industrial and government institutions are also being considered. These steps can be taken to increase the feasibility of LUMI as a start-up.  
The scope of the study is limited to the CALABARZON users for evaluation. However, users across the Philippines can use the system to evaluate and generate renewable energy recommendations for their location. The system have been built with the necessary data for evaluating renewable energy sources on various locations in the Philippines.  
**4.4 Recommendations**   
There have been a number of possible recommendations that can be used to further improve the system capability.  
**4.4.1** Provide recommendations on the hardware. Include ways to estimate the necessary amount of solar panels or dynamos and the ratings to match energy consumption.  
**4.4.2** Add an additional expert mode to allow expert professionals to create hardware layout schematics and simulate its performance.  
**4.4.3** Add a more thorough simulation of solar and wind energy output based on historical data per season instead of averaged historical data.  
**4.4.4** Improve the data used for geothermal energy to give additional depth for analysis and hardware recommendations.  
**4.4.5** Integrate a proper simulation and location validation for geothermal energy location based on local volcanic activity and access to natural hot springs.  
**4.4.6** Allow for a larger scale grid load and energy generation output simulation and recommendation for institutional and government applications.  
**4.4.7** Add AI-powered image based ocular inspection feature to allow for a more accurate recommendation based on local site environment as weather simulation results may not match actual location.  
**4.4.8** Train a dedicated AI model specifically optimized for energy recommendation and result interpretation for novice users instead of relying on commercially available general purpose AI models.  
**4.4.9** Test and validate the system for more locations in the Philippines to ensure accuracy.  
**4.4.10** Develop app for Android, iOS, Windows, and Linux for heavier simulations, expert mode for PC users, and allow for local use without internet.

**Poster** 

**User Manual**

**INTRODUCTION**

**What is LUMI?**  
LUMI: Data-Driven Environmental Intelligence System for Renewable Energy Decision Support is a web-based decision-support system that integrates geospatial, meteorological, infrastructural, and energy-related information. Simply, it is a system designed to provide recommendations on what is the most appropriate renewable energy source based on the location given by the user. It can provide renewable energy source recommendations for household such as solar, wind, hydro, as well as geothermal energy, albeit as a reference for larger scale scenarios. 

Household user can provide their desired location on where they plan to build or want to know the appropriate renewable energy system build. The user could then provide their energy bill and preferred amount of savings. From there, using various regional data that can affect renewable energy output and their feasibility such as climate as geospatial data among others can be taken to account and simulated to create a resulting recommendation. This allows the users to make data-driven decision making related to renewable energy. 

**COMPATIBILITY**

As a web-based system, LUMI’s client side (the website) is compatible with a wide-range of devices provided they have the following:

Device with internet capability

Internet connection with at least 1,638.4 Kbps of download speed, 655.36 Kbps of upload speed, and latency of 150 ms or faster. (Slow 4G speed based on Google Chrome’s Lighthouse testing baseline, average load time of 8.16s)

Web-browsers that are based at least on the following versions or higher are recommended:

Chromium-based (Google Chrome, Opera GX, Microsoft Edge): ver. 126

Mozilla Gecko based (Mozilla Firefox, Zen): ver. 132

Apple Safari: ver. 17.4

**How it works:**

To access LUMI, open a web browser and go to **lumi-frontend-xi.vercel.app**

The navigation bar is at the top right side of the website. This allows the user to navigate various pages in the website, go to the Login/Sign-up page, change the language and color scheme of the website.

In the event that a user opens the website in a device with a vertical display orientation, only the Login button and the hamburger icon are visible. This is normal and it is part of LUMI’s responsive web design for mobile interfaces. 

To reveal the other buttons that have been, tap or click on the hamburger icon. A menu will drop below and will reveal the buttons for Home, About, EcoSim, and Energy Hub. The language and the color scheme selector is also visible. 

By default, the language in LUMI is in English. To change it in Filipino, the user must click on the FIL on the language selector. Clicking EN brings it back to English.

If the user seeks to utilize the EcoSim and Energy Hub functionality, the user must first login to an account. If the user does not have an existing account, the user can login via the Continue with Google button for a convenient single sign-on process. Alternatively, the user can create a new one using the following steps:

Click the login button in the navigation bar. This will take you to the Login/Signup page.  
![][image46]

Click the sign-up button, then fill-in your email and your chosen strong password of at least 8 characters.

Then click create account. A confirmation link will be sent to your email.

Go to your email, then click the link to verify your account.

To login to an existing account made with a user and password:

Go to the Login page

Enter your email and password, then click sign-in

If an account was made using the Continue with Google button. Simply click the button and select the account that you have used if you happen to have multiple Google accounts logged-in to your device.

To recover your forgotten password:

Go to the Login page

Click “Forgot password?” button

![][image47]![][image48]

Fill-in your email address, then click send reset email.

Go to your email to access the reset password page and create a new password.

After the user logs in their account, they will arrive in the user dashboard.

From there, the user can run an EcoSim, view the energy hub, and enable two-factor authentication. The user can also access any saved simulations and saved locations from the dashboard. The user also gets an overview of a municipality by entering a location in the search bar like shown below:

Logging in into an account gives you access to EcoSim and Energy Hub. Additionally, it also modifies the navigation bar to show your profile in place of the log in button.  
Clicking your profile will reveal additional navigation options and actions, these are:  
Dashboard button  
Saved Simulations  
Account Settings  
and the Logout button  
Clicking on the logout button logs you out of LUMI immediately.  
**How to use the EcoSim:**  
Select your desire location by typing it in the search bar or clicking the “Use my location” button. Then click next to proceed.

Enter your electricity on consumption (in KWh), rate per KWh (in ₱/KWh), and your monthly bill (in Philippine Peso or ₱) from you electricity bill. Then click next.  
If you cannot see your rate per KWh, enter your electricity consumption and monthly bill, click the “Use this rate” button. Then click next.

Choose your desired energy savings in percentage by clicking the pre-defined values such as 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%, or by dragging the circle in the slider to select a value from 0% to 100%. Then click next.

If the user wants to include a simple explanation for the results. Mark the checkbox beside the “include a simple explanation”, then proceed to click next.  
Otherwise, remove the check in the checkbox then click next.  
The system will show the user the summary of their inputs. If the user is satisfied with their input, click the run simulation button.  
Otherwise, click the edit button on the input that they wish to edit.

Once the results are ready, a message will appear. Click the view result button to proceed.  
![][image49]![][image50]  
The results would then appear. It is going to show the best match, energy coverage, CO2 reduction, reason for the recommendation, and AI analysis. Scrolling further down shows the renewable energy potential and providers in the area.  
![][image51]![][image52]  
Scrolling even further down shows recommend steps and a button to show technical details. Clicking it shows technical data related to climate and energy output.  
Scrolling back to the top shows the user options to save the results to the account or save it as a PDF.  
**Energy Hub**  
       Energy Hub displays data related to renewable energy, energy demand, national energy source breakdown, renewable energy potential map, energy trends, and overall summary.

**VERBATIM TRANSCRIPT**   
*\[The respondent was provided with the formal letter, study overview, and data privacy statement prior to answering. The respondent consented to participate in this synchronous interview.\]*

*\[Section A \- Data Quality & Sources\]*  
**INTERVIEWER:** As ko lang po yung sa first question po namin — if meron po kayong kino-consider na mga data sources po related doon sa energy sources po.

**RESPONDENT:** Data sources. Well, naka-usap ko na yung isang dating student ko na nag-install ng solar. Sabi niya, meron daw silang pinaghanap na data on the average and peak amount of sunlight received in a certain area. So they also use that data to recommend the proper capacity of solar panel to install based on the needs of the end user. Meron daw silang ganon — kasi bawat lugar iba ang intensity at amount of sunlight.

**INTERVIEWER:** Okay po. So pa-ano niya normally na-validate po, if meron po kayong methods to validate those data po.

**RESPONDENT:** Well, I haven't seen that data, so I cannot validate it. I'm not a solar panel installer. So one thing in doing research is — before you use data, you've already validated it. It's something already given and should not be part of your scope. Unless it's body signals or something with noise, then you have to validate and remove the noise. In terms of this, I think sa tagal na ng mga ganyang renewable energy, there are already valid, reliable sources of data.  The Global Solar Atlas, funded by the World Bank. Data from NASA. Those are data points. I think that's already enough to recommend — you already mention those as your sources and that's it.

**INTERVIEWER:** Sir, meron pa pong ibang data sources na pwede naming kunin maliban lang po sa average sunlight?

**RESPONDENT:** I think meron. Global Solar Atlas, funded by World Bank. Data from NASA. Those are data points already.

**INTERVIEWER:** How should we handle missing data, especially related to energy generation and consumption ng aming users? For example, sometimes may incomplete na information ang ibinibigay nila, or may missing data. How would you normally handle those scenarios to maintain accuracy?

**RESPONDENT:** You can ask as many data and variables as possible. There are some variables that are really relevant — non-negotiable. So the question should not be 'what if walang mako-input na data' because that's already the assumption — you have data. If walang mako-ang data then the premise of this whole research is immaterial.  The data is something that hindi naman kayo ang mag-measure — it is already given. So the next important thing to improve is to talk with a solar panel installer themselves. They would know the actual iterations.

**INTERVIEWER:** Sa tingin niyo po ba meron certain amount ng missing data na pwede na naming i-consider na hindi na siya magagamit?

**RESPONDENT:** Yes, definitely. There are certain variables that are more relevant to the output than others. If may missing, may isa lang missing, papababa yung confidence factor. So your algorithm will suggest — para may confidence factor — kasi may missing data siya. But if you want to increase the confidence, then you put more data.  Sometimes you cannot really get 100% confidence on things — just have to have enough reasons to proceed or not. The algorithm can say: we do recommend installing the solar panel system, but we are only 85% confident on it. Depends on the customer — 85% confident, or 95% confident if the end user is very strict, 99% confidence. The algorithm can only do as much as it can, but still dependent on the end user. So itulayin pa rin na may output, may recommendation, pero may indicator ng confidence level.

**INTERVIEWER:** Do you think there are other environmental variables — like yung bahay niyo, right, malapit po sa sa isang building na kahit po facing south, hindi po fully na-arawan — that need to be considered for the system's decision-making?

**RESPONDENT:** Possible yung pollution index siguro. But I think yung ganun na bagay, I can find an RRL for it. The context is it's very important kasi solar panels need to be cleaned regularly. Dito sa lugar namin, napakadami ng dust, na may time na napanik ng bubong — although very rare — para lang malinis yung mga solar panel namin, para alisin yung hindi kaya ng ulan. Ma-kanon. But I think it's already a minor issue. If you want to put as many variables in degrees of confidence, you can put that kind of environmental variable.

**INTERVIEWER:** Sir, sa granularity po ng data — anong level ng granularity ang preferred? Monthly output, or do you want it more precise, like hourly or daily?

**RESPONDENT:** Monthly na kasi ang bottom line naman ay ang bill ng Meralco — monthly. So yung monthly na total output. Unless yung requirement ng end user is reliability — kasi pag ang requirement is reliability, hindi per-month na yun, lalabas na off-grid kasi. Ang kailangan mo na yung peak consumption per hour at peak production ng solar panel.  So that's how granular it is — it depends on the user. It can be per month, it can be per hour. Pero karamihan, kilowatt hour na yung standard units ng power. Kilowatt hour pwede na.

*\[Section B \- Decision Support Methodology\]*  
**INTERVIEWER:** Ano normally ang mga capabilities na pwede naming gawin? Like do you want forecasting models, trend analysis, or risk assessment sa handling environmental and energy data?

**RESPONDENT:** This is good. For example, malay ba namin kung magtatayo ng malaking building dito sa tabi namin. That could have been a risk factor 10 years ago — what is the possibility na ang kapitbahay namin ay magtatayo ng bahay at tatakpan ang aming bubong? Yes, that's a very possible risk. Good data yun. Pero hindi pa rin ito namo-model ng ganoon.

**RESPONDENT:** Forecasting — trend analysis, prediction — in terms of forecasted future demand ng end user, not the forecasted sunlight. That's already taken in a whole year basis. Forecasting naman dito is — what is the forecasted increase of capacity or demand that the end user would need? Like for example, isama sa forecasting na hybrid na kotse. So isama yun sa forecast — the solar panel system that I would have installed should be scalable. Eventually, kailangan mo na mag-dagdag ng panel eventually in the future.

**INTERVIEWER:** Tapos, if meron po kayong alam na machine learning models or statistical methods na effective sa forecasting?

**RESPONDENT:** Not that I know of. Hindi siya karaniwan gamitin ang AI, in terms of machine learning, for this kind of application.

**INTERVIEWER:** Any multi-criteria decision making methods on top of your mind na pwede naming gamitin?

**RESPONDENT:** Hindi na kuma-ano sa ganyan, pero I think you should find an RRL for it because you want to have as much data, as much reference that is already proven. Unless the purpose of your thesis is to prove that this algorithm can also be used in a different use case — that's a different matter. I doubt that you are proposing a whole new decision analysis matrix. Definitely gagamit kayo ng existing na.  But going back to the point as a devil's advocate — kumeron na nahagawan ng topic ninyo. A research doesn't have to be something that is totally new — it can be a modification of an existing or augmentation of an existing. How do you contextualize it in a Philippine context? Yung mga variables na meron lang sa Pilipinas na hindi naman tinitingnan sa ibang bansa — dito sa Pilipinas importante siya.

**INTERVIEWER:** Di ko na din po siguro itatanong yung how to take into account yung uncertainties kasi parang na mention niyo din po siya sa forecasting models na.

*\[Section C \- System Features & Functionality\]*  
**INTERVIEWER:** Sir, user interface — do you think visually effective visualizations are needed to see the factors affecting possible decisions regarding implementing renewable energy?

**RESPONDENT:** Of course, any visualization is good, but that would make your app or software more complicated. So yun lang — bonus na lang yun. Like for example, kunwari parang 3D rendering ng solar panel system or hanggang sa makita mo ang anino ng kapitbahay or ng mga yari kapag nagtatayo ng sa tabi ng bahay ninyo — although those are very realistic, that should already be beyond your scope, kasi masyadong magiging complicated yung app. Base is already good, no frills na visualization.

**INTERVIEWER:** Okay po. But if for example — dashboards and charts — do you think it will help?

**RESPONDENT:** Yes, of course. Depende sa kung sino ang babasa ng chart. If babasa ay technical person like me, then I would appreciate the technical dashboard. But if yung babasa ng dashboard is a non-technical person, then it's useless to provide all those data. For the regular user, ang kailangan lang ay smiley or sad face or 'not recommended.' Which just signifies recommended or not. For a non-technical person.  So pwede kayong mag-provide ng two types of dashboard — parang basic calculator and scientific calculator. By default, lalabas sa dashboard yung recommendation. Pero if you want to see more data — click here.

**INTERVIEWER:** In terms of providing recommendations, do you prefer it automated na lang siya, or gusto niyo may controls pa rin yung user sa possible values na ibinibigay niya para ma-simulate yung making future?

**RESPONDENT:** Yeah — parang may slider na hinihilahin yung ano, pagbago-bago yung data para makita ko, kung hindi na recommended — ganon.

*\[Section D \- System Performance & Trust\]*  
**INTERVIEWER:** In terms of performance standards — accuracy, response times, and reliability?

**RESPONDENT:** Well, it just needs to be functional. It's not something that you would need to use every now and then. Those kinds of decisions are not decisions that you need to make on a minute-to-minute basis. Those decisions are something that you will only need to make once or twice in your whole life.

**INTERVIEWER:** In terms of accuracy, sir — good starting point or minimum target?

**RESPONDENT:** Well, I'm not a statistician, but as an end user, anything above 90% would be good confidence. But again, you cannot quote me on that — you have to look into RRL.

**INTERVIEWER:** Do you think it would be enough to convince or give assurance to investors or policymakers?

**RESPONDENT:** You have to limit your scope. The end user lang. Why would you need to block policy on solar panel? Why is there a need? Those are more than technical — those are political decisions. If you're talking about barangay-wide or city-wide — companies — that's a very complicated thing to do and already beyond the scope. A lot of factors that you cannot control with that.

**INTERVIEWER:** In terms of validation and transparency — would you like to have an explainable AI system? Would you like to see audit logs or source attributions for the data we use?

**TRANSCRIPT**   
*\[The respondent was provided with the formal letter, study overview, and data privacy statement prior to answering. The respondent consented to participate in this synchronous interview.\]*

*\[Section A: Data Quality & Sources\]*   
**Q1:** What types of environmental and energy data sources do you consider most reliable for renewable energy decision support, and what validation methods should be applied?  
**A1:** For solar irradiance, we mostly use Meteonorm, Solargis, or NASA POWER are the benchmarks. These data sources have wide data ranging from 20 years ago from this year, hence, have more credibility. For grid and energy data, DOE, NGCP and WESM have data on real-time and historical supply and demand of electricity and prices per node. Aside from these, PAGASA for local historical weather extremes and NAMRIA for topographic/elevation data. Some of the validation methods that can be used are range checking (values are physically possible), cross-source comparison, time-series consistency (no spikes from zero to maximum).

**Q2:** Are there emerging data sources (e.g., satellite imagery, crowdsourced data) that you believe should be incorporated?  
**A2:** Google Maps as satellite imagery can also be integrated for shading analysis and rooftop area detection.

**Q3:** How should missing or incomplete energy consumption/generation data be handled in a data-driven intelligence system to maintain prediction accuracy?  
**A3:** For short gaps (1-3 hours), Linear Interpolation can be used. If it's a medium gap (4-24 hours), we can fill the missing data by Same-Day/Previous-Week Matching. Lastly, for very long gaps 9days to weeks), use Regression Modeling or Climatological Averaging. Missing generation data can be filled out using historical solar irradiance from that period.

**Q4:** How do you determine when missing data is too extensive to reliably interpolate versus when it should trigger a system alert?  
**A4:** If it's more than 20% missing or weeks of data it should already trigger a system alert. No need to trigger if only for a few hours as it can be addressed by Linear Interpolation. If it's several days a month worth of data missing, a warning can be triggered instead of an alarm.

**Q5:** What specific environmental and energy data variables (e.g., solar irradiance, wind speed, electricity prices, carbon emissions) do you absolutely need LUMI to track and analyze for your decision-making needs?  
**A5:** Meteorological data needed are Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) (Solar PV yield), Average & Peak Wind Speeds (Wind turbine viability), Daily Rainfall & Head Height (Micro-hydro potential). As for the economic and environmental aspect, Local Utility Retail Rates (PHP/kWh) (for accurate ROI calculation), WESM Node Prices (for community microgrids), Avoided Carbon Emissions (kg CO2) (for environmental impact metrics)

**Q6:** What data resolution (e.g., hourly, daily, monthly) is necessary for each variable to support accurate decisions?  
**A6:** In general, the shorter the data resolution, the better for more accuracy. For solar irradiance, essential to have it an hourly level. If we use a daily or monthly data resolution, it hides the "duck curve". For temperature, daily can be used already (highs and lows), but if possible to have hourly also. For electricity rates & utility bills, monthly data will suffice.

*\[Section B: Decision Support Methodology\]*   
**Q7:** What analytical capabilities (e.g., forecasting models, optimization algorithms, trend analysis, risk assessment) do you need LUMI to perform on environmental and energy data?  
**A7:** I suggest Load and Generation Forecasting, Resource optimization, and risk and resilience assessment.

**Q8:** What specific machine learning or statistical methods (e.g., regression, neural networks, Monte Carlo simulation) have you found most effective for energy forecasting?  
**A8:** For Resource Generation (Solar/Wind): Clear-sky radiation models combined with Random Forest Regression or XGBoost are highly effective. For Energy Demand (Load Profiles): A Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) or SARIMA (Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average). For Financial & Uncertainty Analysis: Monte Carlo Simulations are the industry benchmark. 

**Q9:** Which multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) method (e.g., AHP, Fuzzy AHP, TOPSIS) is most appropriate for renewable energy technology selection, and what criteria should be prioritized?  
**A9:** For technology selection (e.g., choosing whether a community should implement Solar PV, Micro-Hydro, Small Wind, or a Hybrid system), the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) or Fuzzy AHP is highly appropriate. First criteria to be prioritized is the resource availability. if there is no natural resource applicable in that area, it must be eliminated instantly. Next is the economic viability (LCOE, upfront CAPEX) most especially for residential and small communities. Technical and climatic resilience should also be considered most especially for Philippines. Lastly is the land/space constraint. If resource is available on urban areas, is there any land/space available to accommodate this.

**Q10:** What specific weaknesses of your recommended MCDM method have you observed in practice, and how can they be mitigated?  
**A10:** With different renewable energy being evaluated, there's a chance that rank of criteria will be reversed. I suggest implementing TOPSIS as it evaluates alternatives relative to an absolute "ideal" and "anti-ideal" point, eliminating rank reversal entirely.

**Q11:** How should uncertainty in renewable energy forecasts (due to intermittency of solar/wind) be incorporated into the decision support system?  
**A11:** In professional solar engineering, we never present just one generation forecast. We calculate P50 (50% probability the system will generate this much energy—the average) and P90 (90% conservative probability that the system will exceed this production level, representing a poor weather year). The software we are using, PVSyst, already produces these two data.

**Q12:** How should the system adapt uncertainty models when new data reveals that historical patterns no longer apply (e.g., climate change)?  
**A12:** Recency Weighting (Exponential Decay): Modify your statistical and forecasting models to apply a decaying weight to historical data. Weather data from 2020–2026 should carry significantly higher mathematical weight in training your models than data from 1995–2000.

*\[Section C: System Features & Functionality\]*   
**Q13:** What user interface design elements (e.g., dashboards, maps, charts, alerts) do you need for LUMI to effectively visualize environmental and energy data for decision-making?  
**A13:** Geospatial Map Interface showing the resource abundance on that area (e.g., bright orange/red zones for high solar exposure, blue lines indicating nearby river streams with micro-hydro potential). Feasibility scorecards to show simple percentage or qualitative score (e.g., Solar: 92% \- Highly Viable, Wind: 15% \- Not Recommended). It would also be very helpful if there are financial payback & environmental impact meters (e.g. ROI, est. savings, etc.) that can be seen in the interface.

**Q14:** What level of data customization (e.g., filtering by region, time period, technology type) do you need, and how granular should it be?  
**A14:** Geographic wise, if possible, to have the granularity down to the barangay or street level. Hourly for daily profiles; Seasonal (Amihan vs. Habagat) for year-round tracking. 

**Q15:** What level of user interaction (e.g., automated recommendations, manual scenario testing, collaborative planning tools) do you need LUMI to provide for different types of users (households, utilities, policymakers)?  
**A15:** For household mode, interaction level should be primarily automated. Meanwhile, for utility and project developer mode, it should be deeply interactive and parameter-driven simulation (where the user can bypass automated presets and upload custom data). For policymakers, it should be aggregated regional dashboards and macro-simulations is much recommended as they mostly focus on community-scale deployments.

**Q16:** How should LUMI adapt its interface complexity for different user expertise levels (novice vs. expert)?  
**A16:** I suggest having a dual-gate welcome screen which first asks guiding questions to determine expertise level of the user. Jargons relating to renewable energy such as kWp, GHI, LCOE, etc. must also be minimized when the system is on novice screen. If not possible to totally eliminate, wrap them in interactive tooltips that define them inline using simple analogies that they can relate to.

*\[Section D: System Performance & Trust\]*   
**Q17:** What performance standards (e.g., accuracy thresholds, response time, reliability metrics) do you need LUMI to meet to trust and rely on its recommendations for critical energy decisions?  
**A17:** I suggest to split it into two categories: Operational Performance (response time, and system availability), and Analytical Performance (analytical precision thresholds within 5% margin of error, etc)

**Q18:** What minimum accuracy percentage (e.g., 85%, 90%, 95%) do you require for LUMI's predictions before it could be deemed useful for large scale investment or policy decisions?  
**A18:** For household-level decisions, 80% to 85% accuracy is acceptable as these users generally want to have directional guidance on the investment they'll be making. For large-scale investment or policy decisions, system must cross 90-95% accuracy as these have larger CAPEX involved.

**Q19:** What validation and transparency features (e.g., explainable AI, confidence intervals, source attribution, audit logs) do you need LUMI to provide to trust its decision recommendations?  
**A19:** Instead of just showing a final score, the Rule-Based Recommendation Engine should dynamically print out its core rationale using clear conditional text. Build a bounded confidence interval most especially for financial metrics as the data being handled is largely variable. Every chart, calculation, and weather profile must also include an adjacent metadata tag or information hover-state detailing the data origin and its collection timestamp.

**Q20:** What audit or documentation features (e.g., decision history, model version tracking, data change logs) are needed for regulatory compliance or accountability?  
**A20:** Data change logs. Model Version Tracking. When a user saves or exports a configuration report, LUMI should generate a unique, cryptographically hashed Report ID.
